newsitem.title: USA: Senate Democrat leader draws line on tax cut.
newsitem.headline: Senate Democrat leader draws line on tax cut.

text.p: As budget negotiators aim for further progress toward a deal this week, tax cuts remain a big question mark and the leader of Senate Democrats drew a line Monday at $100 billion.
"I couldn't support a $100 billion in tax cuts today, and I would probably oppose a budget agreement that had that much in tax cuts," Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota said.
"We have a lot of members of our caucus who don't believe that under these circumstances that we ought to be cutting taxes at all," he added.

Daschle's comments underscored the fact that even if budget negotiators reached some type of bipartisan agreement, it would still need to be sold to the other members of their respective parties in Congress.
Tax cuts have been a sore spot, and both sides have so far only skimmed the surface in the budget talks. Republicans want a much bigger tax reduction than Democrats.
President Clinton has proposed $98 billion in tax cuts over five years in his budget, while Senate Republicans want up to twice that amount.
Daschle said he would not support any tax reduction that went beyond $100 billion over five years.

"I think it has to stay in the double digits. I don't see ...how we can afford to meet all of our obligations budgetarily, balance the budget by the year 2002, and provide a tax cut in triple digits," he said.
Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth is "looking for significantly more than $100 billion," a spokeswoman for the Delaware Republican said.
Roth heads one of the key tax-writing committees in Congress and has put forth his own plan which seeks about $140 billion in tax relief over five years.

Budget negotiators from the White House and Congress were expected to resume formal talks Wednesday. House and Senate Democrats planned to meet with Clinton at the White House later this week to discuss the budget.
Daschle said the Clinton administration had reassured Democrats it would not give up more savings on the Medicare health programme for the elderly.
The White House offered $18 billion more in Medicare savings during recent budget negotiations to bring total savings to $100 billion over five years. That was a "final offer," Daschle said.
"I think the $100 billion represents the outside parameter, probably the ceiling that is the limit beyond which we simply can't go," Daschle said.

"The administration has indicated to me personally, to the budget committee Democrats, that this is their final offer and I expect that it will be the final offer," he said, referring only to Medicare.
House Democratic Leader Dick Gephardt of Missouri said this weekend he might be able to live with the $100 billion in Medicare cuts, but could not go beyond that.

Asked about Daschle's comments, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said: "We'll continue to be flexible and continue to consult closely with our Democratic friends in Congress, encourage them to understand the need to be flexible, given the reality of what it will take to get an agreement."
The White House was not interested in setting any "artificial deadlines" for reaching a budget deal, McCurry added.
Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers slammed opponents of the U.S. tax system Monday, accusing them of "selfishness".
Summers said most tax cuts should benefit middle income Americans instead of the very wealthy and singled out opponents of the inheritance tax for special criticism.

"I actually think in terms of substantive arguments this estate tax argument is about as bad as it gets," he told a group of reporters at a luncheon, noting the estates of only one percent of Americans were taxed.

"I think there has been a fairly active effort to whip (Americans) into a frenzy over (tax) issues with the agenda of delegitimizing government in general and delegitimizing progressive taxation in particular," he said.
